The federal court’s rules required World Liberty to file a disclosure at the start of the case identifying every one of its owners and where each is a citizen.  World Liberty’s disclosure identified only one entity—World Liberty itself—and listed Florida as its sole citizenship.  Its lawyers certified that they were unaware of anyone else who needed to be disclosed.

World Liberty then moved to compel arbitration, seeking to pull my case out of open court and into secret arbitration proceedings. 

I opposed that motion, and my lawyers spent months and hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting it.  At a hearing in August, the Court signaled that it was not persuaded that my claims belonged in arbitration.  Instead, the Court ruled that certain of my claims should stay in open court, and certain claims should be sent to arbitration, and ordered the parties to meet and confer to come up with a proposed agreement on which claims stay in open court and which ones go to arbitration.

Less than a week later, World Liberty suddenly “corrected” its disclosure.  Where it had previously listed only one member in its ownership chain, it now listed 22, and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE.

Reed Hastings, co-founder of Netflix, on the tension between loyalty and building a great company - his famous "we're a team, not a family" idea.

"We value being nice and we value loyalty, and yet in the workplace, that's a tension.

With loyalty, you would never fire your brother, yet in a company, we lay people off.

All companies used to be family companies. All countries used to be family countries and kingdoms. So it's natural that spills into how we think about an organization.

But the contrast is a professional sports team. Everyone understands that you change players as you need to try to win the championship.

We would say, 'We’re not gonna guarantee you a lot, but we'll guarantee that we'll always surround you with great people and have you work on hard problems.'"

.@reedhastings built Netflix around two ideas that everyone talks about, but are extremely hard to do in practice.

We explore Netflix's content strategy -- why it treats content like a venture portfolio and how it competes with YouTube -- and what Reed learned from serving on the boards of Microsoft, Meta, Anthropic, and Bloomberg.

This is JP Morgan’s view is Wall Street consensus. It assumes there is one Democratic Party. 

My view aligns more with Democrat Strategist Jim Carville, who spoke on the Bulwark podcast two weeks ago. He suggests there are two Democratic parties, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the more moderate/traditional Democrats. These divisions mean the margin of victory might play a huge role in the market’s reaction.
--
Carville:
“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats. That would almost be—I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats win by five because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA. Like, Hakeem [Jeffries] cannot move. He has nowhere to go. Even if you have a close Senate, [Sen. John] Fetterman would keep [Sen. Chuck] Schumer Pepto-Bismol all night. So I think this is one of those races where margin matters a lot.”
--

We would add that if the Senate is a 51-49 Democrat majority, not only does presumed Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer have to worry about PA Senator John Fetterman siding with Republicans, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and a presumed Michigan winner Abdul El-Sayed could put up a “block” because the Democratic Party is not progressive enough.

This issue would come to a head almost immediately over data centers.

Moderate/traditional Democrats, such as unions and middle-class voters, want those jobs. They are accelerationists. 

The DSA wants to block more data center construction. They are decelerationists.

This could turn into an epic fight within the Democratic Party.

posts.name: Manuel Gomes Samuel
posts.text:
France's Debt Problem Is Real. A Eurozone Crisis Is Not Inevitable.

Robin Brooks is right to sound the alarm over France's deteriorating fiscal position. But higher sovereign yields are not synonymous with an impending debt crisis.

France's 10-year borrowing costs now exceed Italy's, yet French debt retains market access, a long maturity profile and substantial investor demand. This looks more like a sharp repricing of country-specific fiscal and political risk than evidence of indiscriminate eurozone contagion.

An oil-price shock could certainly aggravate the situation. But the decisive variable is not oil alone. It is the interaction between growth, debt dynamics, fiscal credibility and the ECB's capacity to contain unjustified fragmentation.

The real danger is when fiscal paralysis turns a manageable debt problem into a self-reinforcing market crisis. That is the distinction policymakers must understand before it is too late.

posts.name: Joseph Toomey
posts.text:
Yes, but the basic problem is the Euro. It is a mechanism that overrode the normal equalizing mechanism that adjusts for structural differences between nations: The Exchange Rate.

For Instance: Previously, before the common currency destroyed the adjustment mechanism, each nation had its own currency that would rise or fall against each other based upon fundamental factors and structural differences. The average Greek retires on a publicly-funded pension at age 54 while a German worker retires at age 67. Some 46% of Greek workers are in the public sector and are funded by 54% who work in the private sector. In Germany, the ratio is closer to 35-65. The Greek budget is continuously in deep deficit while Germans are usually far less profligate.

These huge economic imbalances would normally have been equalized by a declining Drachma and a rising Mark. Now that adjusting function has been overridden.

This causes funds to flow into the Northern Tier economies out of the periphery because Euro-demoninated German assets are on sale while Euro-denominated Greek assets are wildly overpriced.

If the German Central Bank must be relied upon to fund periphery deficits, it's because the rules of the game were rigged in 1992 when this disastrous, unsustainable, absurd common currency mechanism was launched.

Don't cry for Germany. Undo the common currency and restore economic sanity. Then global investors can decide which countries are worth the risk, and which country-specific rate of return levels are justified.
